extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and trainees) performing subject-matter eligibility (§101) analyses
extracted.subtask_description: A worksheet for analyzing patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (judicial exceptions: law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance; steps guide examiners through identifying the invention, statutory category, whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), and whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and establish BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be brief and should not just reproduce the claim. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section I: summarize applicant's invention in plain terms focused on what the invention accomplishes (examples given: managing Bingo game aspects, performance guaranty, distribution of media by advertising). Emphasize that every claim must be examined individually and the summary should not simply restate the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A (Yes) or B (No). If No, make a rejection as drawn to non‑statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption, make the assumption clear in the record, and consider suggesting a potential amendment to applicant that would result in the claim being drawn to a statutory category. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Is the claim directed to an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a concept similar to those identified by courts as abstract (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, mathematical relationships/formulae). A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A (No), B (Yes — but a streamlined analysis is appropriate), or C (Yes — identify the limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain why). Use the case law chart and 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. If streamlined (B) is appropriate, a full eligibility analysis may not be needed (see February 2015 Training Slides). If C, explicitly identify the claim elements that set forth the abstract idea and explain why those elements constitute an abstract idea (examples provided in worksheet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claim limitations that recite the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: List the specific claim elements/limitations (steps, components) that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why those limitations are considered the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each claim, enumerate the elements that embody the abstract idea (example: Bingo example lists elements (i)–(viii) such as input of preselected numbers, storage as a group, assignment of player identifier, retrieval, selection for play, addition of control number, output of receipt, verification via control number). Then explain why the described scheme is an abstract idea (e.g., organizing human activity, can be performed mentally or with a computer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Are there additional elements beyond the abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim includes any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the abstract idea identified in Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 (No) or 2 (Yes). If No (no other elements), conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue examination under other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If Yes, list the additional claim elements (e.g., computer with CPU, memory, printer, input/output, program) and continue to evaluate their significance under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the significance of additional elements (search for an 'inventive concept')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, confer an 'inventive concept' such that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the additional elements relate to what the applicant invented and evaluate them both individually and in combination. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following considerations: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions and not mere instructions to implement the idea on a computer); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (i.e., not appending well‑understood routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment. It is not important how many of these considerations apply; evaluate significance relative to applicant's invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes insufficient 'additional elements' (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on common deficient recitations that do not amount to 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of insufficient elements include: providing a programmed/generic computer performing generic computer functions; mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent; appending well‑understood, routine and conventional activities at a high level of generality; adding insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering. If additional elements are only generic computer components claimed to perform basic storage/retrieval/processing functions, they likely do not add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural: Suggest potential claim amendments and document assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If elements in the disclosure could be added to make the claim eligible, identify those elements and consider suggesting them to applicant; if analyzing under an assumed amendment, make the assumption clear in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet fields prompt examiners to identify possible disclosure elements that could be added and to note them in the Office action. If the examiner continues analysis based on an assumed amendment (e.g., to place the claim into a statutory category), explicitly state the assumption in the record and consider proposing specific amendments to applicant. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and proceed to other requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official form paragraphs for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that a claim is ineligible under §101, use the designated form paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 where applicable) available in Custom OACs when making a §101 rejection. Sample rejection language is provided in the worksheet demonstrating how to explain that the claim is 'directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more' and why additional elements are insufficient.
